issues.legal_issue: A requirement that a completed sale be registered does not bar a transferee from relying on part performance of a contract of sale to defend possession.
material_facts: The owner sued to recover possession of land and a factory from a purchaser who had entered possession under a written agreement to sell.
The purchaser relied on the agreement and the equitable defense of part performance, not on a completed sale or conveyance.
The agreement was signed by the owner, and the purchaser had taken possession and made a part payment.
issues.conclusion: The registration requirement for a sale did not bar the purchaser from relying on the defense of part performance.
issues.legal_principle: Section 70(8) of the Madhya Bharat Land Revenue and Tenancy Act, 1950 required registration before a sale under that section could be deemed valid. It did not apply to a defense founded on a contract of sale where no sale had occurred. Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act permits a transferee meeting its requirements to defend possession against the transferor.

rule.if: owner_possession_claim and written_signed_sale_contract and no_completed_sale and possession_defense_based_on_contract

predicates.owner_possession_claim: An owner brought a proceeding to recover possession of property from a person in possession.
predicates.written_signed_sale_contract: The parties made a written contract to transfer the property for consideration, signed by the transferor and containing ascertainable transfer terms.
predicates.no_completed_sale: The transfer had not been completed as a sale or conveyance.
predicates.possession_defense_based_on_contract: The person in possession relied on the contract and part performance, rather than on a completed sale, to resist the possession claim.

issues.definition: When an owner seeks possession from someone who relies on a signed sale contract and part performance, and no sale has been completed, the registration requirement for a sale does not bar that defense.

issues.legal_issue: A transferee is willing to perform a contract when the transferor's obligations fall due first and the transferee has arranged to pay the balance, even if the balance has not been paid by its stated due date.
material_facts: The purchaser had not paid the balance by the stated due date and had not made the pleaded tender.
The agreement required the owner to have his brother's name removed from the revenue records, and the owner had not done so before rescinding the contract.
The court treated obtaining the required official sanction as an implied condition of the agreement; the owner had not obtained it.
The purchaser had arranged financing sufficient to pay the balance, and the agreement's sequence required the owner to perform his obligations before the purchaser could be called on to pay.
issues.conclusion: The purchaser was at all relevant times willing to perform his part of the contract and could not be required to pay the balance before the owner performed his earlier obligations.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act, the transferee must have performed or be willing to perform his part of the contract. Section 4 of that Act makes its contract-related provisions part of the Indian Contract Act, 1872; the sequence of contractual obligations therefore matters, and a party cannot demand performance of a later obligation before performing its own earlier obligation. Where a statute requires permission to transfer property, the agreement is subject to an implied condition that the transferor obtain permission: Motilal v. Nanhelal and Mrs. Chandhee Widya Vati Madden v. Dr. C. L. Katial. A purchaser need not necessarily produce the money or prove a concluded financing scheme to establish readiness: Bank of India Ltd. v. Jamsetji A. H. Chinoy.

rule.if: part_performance_defense_case and balance_unpaid_by_due_date and transferor_prior_obligations_unperformed and transferor_obligations_precede_payment and transferee_financing_arranged

predicates.part_performance_defense_case: A transferee relied on part performance to defend possession against a claim by the transferor.
predicates.balance_unpaid_by_due_date: The transferee did not pay the contractual balance by the stated due date.
predicates.transferor_prior_obligations_unperformed: The transferor had not completed obligations required of the transferor under the agreement, including an express obligation and an implied prerequisite to transfer.
predicates.transferor_obligations_precede_payment: The agreement's sequence of performance required the transferor to complete those obligations before the transferee had to pay the balance.
predicates.transferee_financing_arranged: The transferee had made arrangements to obtain the funds needed to pay the balance.

issues.definition: In a part-performance defense, when the balance is unpaid but the transferor has not completed obligations that must precede payment and the transferee has arranged the funds, the transferee is willing to perform.

issues.legal_issue: Acts done in part performance need not be independent of the terms of the contract.
material_facts: The purchaser took possession of the property under the written agreement.
The purchaser made a part payment in pursuance of the agreement.
The owner argued that an act in furtherance of the contract had to be independent of the contract's terms.
issues.conclusion: The purchaser's acts in pursuance of the contract could satisfy the requirement of an act in furtherance; they did not have to be independent of the contract's terms.
issues.legal_principle: Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act requires an act in furtherance of the contract, but the act need not be independent of the contract's terms. The Court held that the written agreement, the purchaser's possession, and the part payment satisfied the first three requirements for the defense.

predicates.part_performance_defense_case: A transferee relied on part performance to defend possession against a claim by the transferor.
predicates.possession_taken_under_contract: The transferee took possession of the property in performance of the contract.
predicates.payment_made_under_contract: The transferee made a payment in pursuance of the contract.

issues.definition: When a transferee defending possession took possession and made a payment under the contract, those acts may further the contract without being independent of its terms.

issues.legal_issue: Repeal of the law imposing a permission requirement does not retrospectively remove that requirement from an earlier contract subject to it.
material_facts: The contract was subject to an implied requirement that the transferor obtain official sanction for the transfer.
The sanction was not obtained before the earlier law was repealed.
The court rejected the contention that the repeal operated retrospectively.
issues.conclusion: The repeal did not operate retrospectively, and the earlier permission requirement remained relevant to the contract.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that repeal of the Madhya Bharat Land Revenue and Tenancy Act, 1950 by the Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, 1959 did not have retrospective operation. It also applied the principle, supported by Motilal v. Nanhelal and Mrs. Chandhee Widya Vati Madden v. Dr. C. L. Katial, that an agreement to transfer property restricted by statute is subject to an implied condition that the transferor obtain the required sanction.

rule.if: contract_performance_dispute and contract_subject_to_permission_requirement and permission_not_obtained_before_repeal and later_law_repealed_earlier_requirement

predicates.contract_performance_dispute: A dispute concerns performance of a contract to transfer property.
predicates.contract_subject_to_permission_requireme: The contract was subject to a requirement that the transferor obtain official permission for the transfer.
predicates.permission_not_obtained_before_repeal: The required permission had not been obtained before the relevant law was repealed.
predicates.later_law_repealed_earlier_requirement: A later law repealed the earlier law that imposed the permission requirement.

issues.definition: In a contract performance dispute, if the contract was subject to permission that remained unobtained when the requiring law was repealed, the repeal does not retrospectively remove that requirement.
